title: I-1 Light Industrial Warehouse with Office Component
brief: A manufacturing company proposes a 3-storey light industrial warehouse facility on a 2,000 sqm rectangular site zoned I-1 (Light Industrial). Site frontage is 40m (south-facing) with 50m depth. The ground floor features a high-bay warehouse with 6.0m clear height for storage and a mezzanine office level (400 sqm), plus two loading bays facing the street. The 2nd floor accommodates light manufacturing/assembly, while the 3rd floor provides administrative offices. A 4m drainage easement along the west boundary and a 15m right-of-way abutting the south frontage must be observed. Site regulations: PSO 70%, BHL 15m, FLAR 1.5–2.5, RROW 15m, ISA 15%, USA 15%, 1% toward RROW. Adjacent uses: industrial (east), drainage canal (west), commercial (north/rear). Determine plot development potential, setback compliance, and floor area optimization.

program.building_type: Light Industrial Warehouse with Office Component
required_spaces: Warehouse storage with 6.0m clear height (ground floor)
Administrative offices, meeting rooms, pantry, toilets (3rd floor)
special_requirements: Mezzanine does not count as additional floor (less than 1/3 of ground floor area)
2 loading bays with truck maneuvering area
Street-facing loading permitted in I-1 zone

computation_sheet.governing_constraint: Drainage easement (4m) on west side governs over 3.0m side setback

hidden_traps.title: Building Height Bracket Change Due to Warehouse Ground Floor
hidden_traps.description: Building height is 12.5m (not 9.0m) due to 6.5m warehouse ground floor — triggers the 12-15m setback bracket instead of the up-to-9m bracket. Students who assume all floors are 3.0m (9.0m total) will use wrong setback values, gaining extra buildable width.
hidden_traps.consequence: Wrong setbacks lead to incorrect AMBF calculation and false compliance.

hidden_traps.title: Drainage Easement Overrides Standard Side Setback
hidden_traps.description: Drainage easement (4m) on west side governs over the 3.0m side setback — students who ignore easement get wider buildable area (40m - 3.0m - 3.0m = 34m instead of correct 33m).
hidden_traps.consequence: Ignoring easement inflates buildable footprint area by 1.0m on one dimension, leading to false floor area optimization.

hidden_traps.title: Mezzanine Does Not Count as Additional Floor for TGFA
hidden_traps.description: Mezzanine (400 sqm) is less than 1/3 of ground floor area (900 sqm) — does NOT count as additional floor for TGFA. Students may incorrectly add 400 sqm to TGFA, inflating total to 4,459 instead of correct 4,059 sqm.
hidden_traps.consequence: Inflated TGFA leads to wrong FLAR, parking/loading requirements, and false zoning compliance.

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Allowable Building Footprint (AMBF) from the Plot Setback Ordinance (PSO = 70%). What is the maximum allowed built area at ground level?

rationale.correct: PSO = 70%. AMBF = Lot Area × PSO = 2,000 × 0.70 = 1,400 sqm.
rationale.distractor_1: Partial calculation (missing final multiplication or using 75%).
rationale.distractor_2: Uses I-2 PSO of 84% incorrectly: 2,000 × 0.84 = 1,680 sqm.
rationale.takeaway: Always verify development control values against the correct zone classification in Table VII.G.1.

questions.takeaway: PSO is zone-specific. I-1 explicitly = 70%. Do not confuse with other industrial or commercial zones.
questions.code_citation: NLC Zoning Code § I-1.02(b) — Plot Setback Ordinance for Light Industrial

questions.question_stem: For this I-1 industrial site, the building height is determined by the warehouse ground floor clear height of 6.0m plus floor-to-floor overlays. Calculate the actual total building height. Ground floor floor-to-floor = 6.5m; typical floors = 3.0m each.

rationale.correct: Total height = 6.5 (ground FTF) + 3.0 (2nd) + 3.0 (3rd) = 12.5 m. This falls in the 'over 12m to 15m' setback bracket, NOT 'up to 9m'.
rationale.distractor_0: Trap 1: Assumes all floors = 3.0m (3 × 3.0 = 9.0m). Ignores the 6.5m warehouse ground floor. This leads to wrong setback values.
rationale.distractor_1: Adds only ground + one typical floor (6.5 + 3.0 = 9.5m), missing one floor.
rationale.takeaway: Always verify development control values against the correct zone classification in Table VII.G.1.

questions.takeaway: TRAP 1: Warehouse ground floors have tall clear heights (6.0–8.0m). Always check the brief for actual FTF dimensions, not generic 3.0m. This changes the setback bracket entirely.
solution_steps: Identify ground floor FTH: 6.5m (stated in brief as 6.0m clear height + slab)
Use appropriate setback values for this bracket
questions.code_citation: NLC Zoning Code § I-1.04(c) — Height & Setback Brackets; Warehouse FTH Standard § WH.02

questions.question_stem: Using the correct building height (12.5m), determine the front setback from the RROW (south-facing). Setback table: up to 9m = 4.5m, over 9m to 12m = 5.25m, over 12m to 15m = 6.0m.

rationale.correct: Building height = 12.5m → bracket 'over 12m to 15m' → front setback = 6.0m.
rationale.distractor_0: Uses 'up to 9m' bracket (4.5m) if student wrongly calculated height as 9.0m. TRAP 1 consequence.
rationale.distractor_1: Uses 'over 9m to 12m' bracket (5.25m) if student calculated height as ~10.5m (missing one floor or underestimating).
rationale.distractor_2: Adds arbitrary 1.5m buffer to the correct 6.0m value.
rationale.takeaway: Setback brackets depend on actual building height, not the standard 3.0m × floors assumption.

questions.takeaway: Setback values depend critically on correct building height. The height bracket is non-linear. One wrong assumption cascades.
solution_steps: Consult setback table for 'over 12m to 15m' bracket
questions.code_citation: NLC Zoning Code § I-1.05(a) — Setback Schedule by Height Bracket

questions.question_stem: The site has a 4m drainage easement along the west boundary. Standard side setback for the 12.5m building height is 3.0m. Which setback governs the west side buildable limit?

rationale.correct: Easement takes priority. A 4m easement is more restrictive than a 3.0m setback. The building must stay 4.0m from the west boundary. TRAP 2: Students ignoring the easement use only the 3.0m setback, gaining an extra 1.0m width.
rationale.distractor_0: Uses setback only, ignoring easement. This leads to buildable area = 40 - 3.0 - 3.0 = 34m, not 33m.
rationale.distractor_1: Tries to split the difference, not how zoning works.
rationale.distractor_2: Misinterprets easement as allowing setback reduction.
rationale.takeaway: Setback brackets depend on actual building height, not the standard 3.0m × floors assumption.

questions.takeaway: TRAP 2: Always check for easements, encroachments, and deed restrictions. They often override standard setbacks and dictate actual buildable limits.
solution_steps: Identify standard side setback for 12.5m height: 3.0m
Easement governs → use 4.0m from west boundary
questions.code_citation: NLC Zoning Code § I-1.05(b) — Side Setbacks; § Easement.01 — Easement Priority Over Setback

questions.question_stem: Calculate the buildable ground floor footprint considering all setbacks: front 6.0m, rear 3.0m, east 3.0m, west 4.0m (easement). Lot is 40m × 50m.

rationale.correct: Buildable width (E-W) = 40 − 3.0 − 4.0 = 33m. Buildable depth (N-S) = 50 − 6.0 − 3.0 = 41m. Area = 33 × 41 = 1,353 sqm. This is MORE restrictive than AMBF (1,400 sqm), so setbacks govern.
rationale.distractor_0: Uses wrong rear setback (2.0m instead of 3.0m) or ignores easement. 40 − 3.0 − 3.0 = 34m width → 34 × 38 = 1,292 sqm.
rationale.distractor_1: Uses 3.0m side setbacks on both sides, ignoring easement: 40 − 3.0 − 3.0 = 34m. Then 50 − 6.0 − 3.0 = 41m → 34 × 41 = 1,394 sqm (close, but wrong).
rationale.distractor_2: Uses AMBF from PSO without checking setbacks: 1,400 sqm.
rationale.takeaway: Setback brackets depend on actual building height, not the standard 3.0m × floors assumption.

questions.takeaway: Always compute buildable area from BOTH PSO and setbacks. The MORE restrictive value governs. Easements reduce buildable width.
solution_steps: Compare to AMBF: 1,353 sqm < 1,400 sqm → setbacks are limiting factor
questions.code_citation: NLC Zoning Code § Setback.02 — Buildable Area Determination

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Impervious Surface Area (ISA) requirement. ISA = 15% of lot area. What is the maximum allowable ISA in sqm?

rationale.takeaway: Always verify development control values against the correct zone classification in Table VII.G.1.

questions.takeaway: ISA includes parking, driveways, hardstand, loading areas. Verify the exact percentage in the brief.
questions.code_citation: NLC Zoning Code § I-1.03(d) — Impervious Surface Area Limits

questions.question_stem: Calculate the total Unbuilt Soft Area (USA) requirement. USA = 15% of lot area. What is the maximum allowable USA in sqm?

rationale.takeaway: Always verify development control values against the correct zone classification in Table VII.G.1.

questions.takeaway: USA is landscaping, green space, gardens, water features. Combined with ISA, MACA = ISA% + USA% defines maximum covered + soft area.
questions.code_citation: NLC Zoning Code § I-1.03(e) — Unbuilt Soft Area Requirements

questions.question_stem: Calculate Total Open Space Land (TOSL) by summing ISA and USA. What is TOSL?

rationale.distractor_1: Adds one of them to the PSO area incorrectly: ~550 sqm.
rationale.distractor_2: Over-counts by using different percentages or doubling.
rationale.takeaway: Always verify development control values against the correct zone classification in Table VII.G.1.

questions.takeaway: TOSL is the sum of ISA and USA. Remaining lot = Total lot − TOSL − Building footprint.
questions.code_citation: NLC Zoning Code § Open Space.01 — TOSL Definition

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Maximum Allowable Coverage Area (MACA) as a percentage. MACA = PSO% + ISA%. What is MACA?

rationale.correct: MACA = PSO + ISA = 70% + 15% = 85% of the lot may be covered (building + pavement).
rationale.distractor_1: Uses PSO + USA instead: 70% + 15% = 85% (but this conflates coverage with soft area).
rationale.takeaway: Always verify development control values against the correct zone classification in Table VII.G.1.

questions.takeaway: MACA = hardscape + building. USA is separate. Remaining permeable area = 100% − MACA − USA.
questions.code_citation: NLC Zoning Code § Coverage.01 — MACA Calculation

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Total Gross Floor Area (TGFA) for the 3-storey building. Ground footprint = 1,353 sqm (after setbacks). Mezzanine = 400 sqm (within ground floor). Note: A mezzanine counts as an additional floor only if it exceeds 1/3 of the floor below. What is TGFA?

rationale.correct: Mezzanine = 400 sqm out of 1,353 sqm ground floor = 29.6%, which is LESS than 33.3% (1/3). Mezzanine does NOT count as a separate floor. TGFA = 1,353 × 3 floors = 4,059 sqm.
rationale.distractor_0: TRAP 3: Counts mezzanine as additional floor (1,353 × 3) + 400 = 4,459 sqm. This is incorrect because mezzanine < 1/3.
rationale.distractor_1: Over-inflates by adding mezzanine AND using wrong footprint or floor count: ~5,412 sqm.
rationale.distractor_2: Adds mezzanine to a partial calculation: 1,353 × 3 + some adjustment = ~5,059 sqm.
rationale.takeaway: Always verify development control values against the correct zone classification in Table VII.G.1.

questions.takeaway: TRAP 3: Mezzanines are tricky. They count as a separate floor ONLY if > 1/3 of the floor area below. Always verify the ratio. Common mistake: counting every mezzanine as a floor.
solution_steps: Identify ground footprint after setbacks: 1,353 sqm
Check if mezzanine counts: 400 ÷ 1,353 = 29.6% < 33.3% → does NOT count
questions.code_citation: NLC Building Code § Floor.02 — Mezzanine Floor Area Threshold (1/3 rule)

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Floor-to-Area Ratio (FLAR) for this project. FLAR = TGFA ÷ Lot Area. Allowable range = 1.5–2.5. Does the project meet the FLAR requirement?

rationale.correct: FLAR = 4,059 ÷ 2,000 = 2.03. This is within the 1.5–2.5 range.
rationale.distractor_0: Uses wrong TGFA (e.g., 3,780 sqm from an earlier calculation error): 3,780 ÷ 2,000 = 1.89.
rationale.distractor_1: Uses TGFA with mezzanine counted: 4,459 ÷ 2,000 = 2.23 (exceeds max but students may think it's OK).
rationale.distractor_2: Adds extra layers or miscalculates footprint: ~4,900 ÷ 2,000 = 2.45.
rationale.takeaway: Always verify development control values against the correct zone classification in Table VII.G.1.

questions.takeaway: FLAR is a density control. Always verify against the zoning range. If FLAR exceeds max, the design is non-compliant (height or footprint must be reduced).
questions.code_citation: NLC Zoning Code § I-1.06 — Floor Area Ratio Limits

questions.question_stem: What is the maximum building height limit (BHL) for this I-1 zone, and does the 12.5m building height comply?

rationale.correct: BHL = 15m (stated in brief). Building height = 12.5m ≤ 15m ✓ Compliant.
rationale.distractor_0: Misreads BHL as 12m (confuses with 12m setback bracket) → 12.5m exceeds.
rationale.distractor_1: Uses residential zone BHL (18m) by error → building complies but so does any I-1 building under 15m.
rationale.distractor_2: Uses restricted I-2 or commercial BHL of 10m → 12.5m exceeds.
rationale.takeaway: Always verify development control values against the correct zone classification in Table VII.G.1.

questions.takeaway: BHL is zone-specific. Always confirm the exact limit from the brief or code. Don't conflate setback brackets with height limits.
questions.code_citation: NLC Zoning Code § I-1.04(a) — Building Height Limit

questions.question_stem: The loading dock is located on the ground floor facing the south (street-facing RROW). In an I-1 light industrial zone, is this placement compliant with typical warehouse zoning?
options: Yes, loading docks must face the public right-of-way
Yes, street-facing loading is standard practice and improves traffic flow
No, loading docks must be internal or screened from public view in I-1 zones
No, loading docks cannot be within 6m of the property line

rationale.correct: In I-1 light industrial, street-facing loading docks are acceptable and standard. They provide efficient access from the street. No screening requirement is imposed for I-1 (stricter in residential/commercial zones).
rationale.distractor_0: Over-states the requirement as 'must' face RROW, when really it's permitted but not mandatory.
rationale.distractor_1: Confuses I-1 with residential or mixed-use zones where loading must be screened.
rationale.distractor_2: Applies a distance restriction (6m) that applies to other uses, not loading docks in I-1.
rationale.takeaway: Space planning decisions must align with the building program and code requirements.

questions.takeaway: Loading dock placement rules vary by zone. I-1 is industrial-friendly; residential/commercial zones impose screening. Always check zoning restrictions for specific uses.
solution_steps: Check I-1 loading dock rules: Street-facing permitted (efficient for trucks)
questions.code_citation: NLC Zoning Code § I-1.07(b) — Loading Dock & Service Yard Requirements

questions.question_stem: The 3rd floor contains administrative offices. The adjacent north property (rear) is zoned commercial. Is this adjacency compatible under I-1 zoning, and are there any required buffer or soundproofing measures?
options: No compatibility issue; no additional measures required
Compatible, but a 2m buffer zone must be maintained on the north boundary
Incompatible; office use must be relocated to the ground floor or rear building
Compatible, but STC (sound transmission class) ≥ 60 required in north-facing walls

rationale.correct: I-1 light industrial and commercial are adjacent uses. Both are industrial/commercial zones with similar noise/activity tolerances. No buffer or soundproofing required. They are compatible.
rationale.distractor_0: Applies buffer zone requirement (2m) used for industrial-to-residential adjacency, not commercial adjacency.
rationale.distractor_1: Assumes offices in I-1 are incompatible with commercial zones. I-1 explicitly allows office components. Both zones tolerate industrial activity.
rationale.distractor_2: Applies STC requirement used for residential-adjacent industrial, not commercial-adjacent.
rationale.takeaway: Space planning decisions must align with the building program and code requirements.

questions.takeaway: Adjacency compatibility depends on zone pairs. Industrial-industrial and industrial-commercial are usually compatible. Residential adjacency requires buffers and soundproofing.
solution_steps: Check compatibility matrix for I-1 + Commercial: Compatible ✓
Check for buffer/soundproofing requirements: None for commercial adjacency
questions.code_citation: NLC Zoning Code § I-1.08(a) — Adjacency Compatibility; § Buffer.01 — Industrial-Residential Buffer Requirements

questions.question_stem: Classify this 3-storey light industrial warehouse building under the building code fire zone system. Which fire zone classification applies?

rationale.correct: A 3-storey warehouse with non-combustible structural frame (steel assumed) falls into Fire Zone B. Multi-storey industrial buildings with robust structural systems are classified B.
rationale.distractor_0: Fire Zone C applies to smaller or single-storey combustible warehouses. This building is 3 storeys with structural redundancy.
rationale.distractor_1: Fire Zone A is commercial/high-rise, not industrial.
rationale.distractor_2: Fire Zone D is not a standard classification.
rationale.takeaway: Building design knowledge questions test real professional decisions architects make on projects.

questions.takeaway: Building code fire zones depend on occupancy, height, area, and structural system. Industrial warehouses are typically B or C. Multi-storey non-combustible = Zone B.
solution_steps: Identify structural system: Steel frame (typical for warehouses)
Fire Zone Classification: B (multi-storey non-combustible industrial)
questions.code_citation: NLC Building Code § Fire Zones.02 — Fire Zone Classification Table; § IBC 2206.01 — Warehouse Occupancy

questions.question_stem: For the ground floor warehouse with 6.0m clear height, what structural system is most appropriate and economical?
options: Reinforced concrete frame with deep beams (cost-inefficient)
Steel frame with open-web joists or composite deck (standard warehouse solution)
Timber trusses (inadequate for 6m span and live loads)

rationale.correct: Steel frame with composite deck or open-web joists provides efficient span capability, easy integration of MEP, and rapid construction. Standard for warehouses.
rationale.distractor_0: Reinforced concrete CAN work but requires deeper sections (more weight, cost). Less flexible for future modification.
rationale.distractor_1: Timber trusses cannot span 6m+ with typical warehouse loads (forklift, racking, palletized goods at 5+ kN/sqm).
rationale.distractor_2: Post-tensioned is over-engineered and expensive for a simple warehouse span.
rationale.takeaway: Structural system selection must match the building type, span, and load requirements.

questions.takeaway: Warehouse clear height demands efficient long-span structure. Steel is industry standard. Choose joists/deck type based on span and live load.
solution_steps: Identify live loads: Racking + forklifts = 5–7 kN/sqm
Evaluate structural options: Steel frame best for economy and flexibility
Specify: Steel frame with composite/metal deck
questions.code_citation: NLC Building Code § Structural.03 — Warehouse Structural Systems; AISC Steel Design Guide

questions.question_stem: The loading dock has 2 bays for truck access. Standard truck loading bay width and depth are 3.5m × 15m per bay. What is the total area occupied by the loading dock (including circulation and maneuvering)?

rationale.correct: 2 bays × (3.5m × 15m) = 2 × 52.5 = 105 sqm. Add maneuvering area (truck turnaround, staging): ~75 sqm additional. Total ≈ 180 sqm.
rationale.distractor_0: Counts bay area only (105 sqm), omitting maneuvering and staging zones.
rationale.distractor_2: Over-estimates by including excessive circulation: 210 sqm.
rationale.takeaway: Interior dimensions must meet applicable standards and code minimums.

questions.takeaway: Loading docks include bays PLUS maneuvering areas. Truck turnarounds, staging zones, and canopy coverage add 30–50% to gross bay area.
solution_steps: Maneuvering/staging/canopy = ~75 sqm (14-point turn truck turnaround, queue staging)
questions.code_citation: ITE Loading Bay Design Standards; NLC Warehouse Code § WH.05 — Loading Area Dimension Requirements

questions.question_stem: The ground floor warehouse will have a reinforced concrete slab-on-grade. Assume a bearing capacity of 20 kN/sqm for the soil, and expected live load from racking + equipment = 50 kN/sqm. The slab must be designed for a concentrated load from a racking column = 300 kN on a 0.5m × 0.5m footprint. What minimum slab thickness is required (assuming f'c = 30 MPa concrete)?

rationale.correct: Using slab design for racking loads (ACI 360, Warehouse Design): t = √(P / (φ × c × f'c)) where P = 300 kN, φ = 0.9, c ≈ 0.9 (bearing factor). t ≈ 240–260 mm → specify 250 mm. Alternatively, using 50 kN/sqm distributed live load and bearing checks, t ≥ 200 mm; concentrated load bumps to 250 mm.
rationale.distractor_0: 150 mm is typical for light storage or parking (15 kN/sqm live load), not heavy warehouse racking.
rationale.distractor_1: 200 mm is minimal for general warehouse (30–40 kN/sqm) but insufficient for concentrated 300 kN racking loads.
rationale.distractor_2: 300 mm is over-designed and uneconomical for this load case.
rationale.takeaway: Material quantity computations must account for waste and construction tolerances.

questions.takeaway: Warehouse slabs must accommodate both distributed live loads (racking) AND concentrated point loads (individual racking feet). Always check both; the higher governs.
solution_steps: Identify concentrated load: 300 kN (racking column foot)
Check distributed load governs: 50 kN/sqm → t ≈ 200 mm (standard warehouse)
Check concentrated load governs: 300 kN on 0.5m × 0.5m → bearing stress = 300 ÷ (0.5 × 0.5) = 1,200 kPa
Apply ACI 360 concentrated load formula or spreadsheet: t ≈ 240–250 mm required
Specify: 250 mm reinforced concrete slab-on-grade, f'c = 30 MPa, with dowels for racking foot loads
questions.code_citation: ACI 360 Report — Design of Slabs-on-Grade; NLC Building Code § Concrete.04 — Warehouse Slab Design; IFI Racking Code § Load Cell Design

questions.question_stem: Calculate the required parking and loading spaces for this facility. Use ITE standards: light industrial warehouse = 3 spaces per 1,000 sqm GFA; loading = 1 space per 1,000 sqm GFA, minimum 2 spaces. TGFA = 4,059 sqm. How many total parking + loading spaces are required?

rationale.correct: Parking: (4,059 ÷ 1,000) × 3 = 12.18 ≈ 12 spaces. Loading: (4,059 ÷ 1,000) × 1 = 4.06 spaces, but minimum = 2 spaces (given: 'minimum 2'). Total = 12 + 2 = 14 spaces. (The brief specifies 2 loading bays; requirement is 2 spaces minimum, so 2 is OK.)
rationale.distractor_0: Under-counts parking (8 instead of 12) and uses minimum loading (2) → 10 total.
rationale.distractor_1: Counts parking correctly (12) but mistakenly uses 1 loading space (misreads minimum rule).
rationale.distractor_2: Over-counts loading by using 4 spaces (full formula without recognizing 2-bay constraint and minimum rule).
rationale.takeaway: Parking and loading requirements depend on building use, floor area, and occupancy.

questions.takeaway: Parking and loading are separate requirements. Always apply the formula, then check minimums/maximums. Brief-specific details (number of loading bays) may define the actual provision.
solution_steps: Loading requirement: (4,059 ÷ 1,000) × 1 = 4.06 spaces, but minimum 2 spaces
Project has 2 loading bays (stated in brief) → use 2 loading spaces
questions.code_citation: ITE Parking Generation Manual (6th Ed.) — Light Industrial Warehouse; NLC Zoning Code § I-1.09 — Parking & Loading Requirements
